Machine Proofs for Adams Differentials and Extension Problems Among CW Spectra

Weinan Lin, Guozhen Wang and Zhouli Xu
Abstract.

In this document, we describe the process of obtaining numerous Adams differentials and extensions using computational methods, as well as how to interpret the dataset uploaded to Zenodo [6]. Detailed proofs of the machine-generated results are also provided. The dataset includes information on 49 CW spectra, 180 maps, and 61 cofiber sequences. Leveraging these results, and with the addition of some ad hoc arguments derived through human insight, we successfully resolved the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem in dimension 126 [7].

1. Introduction

In this project, we first compute the Adams E2E_{2}-pages and maps for many CW spectra using the computer program ./Adams, developed by the first author [4]. All relevant spectra and maps have been uploaded to the Zenodo repository [6] and are described in detail in Section 2. Additionally, another program, ./ss, also developed by the first author [4], computes Adams differentials and extensions. The resulting data are included in the Zenodo repository and described in Section 3.

The program ./ss also generates proofs for all computed results, which are organized into a comprehensive resource we refer to as the Table of Proofs. This program partially employs the Generalized Leibniz Rule and the Generalized Mahowald Trick—two theorems established in the paper [7] addressing the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem. These theorems enable the program to derive new differentials and extensions from previously computed ones. Detailed instructions on how to interpret and navigate the Table of Proofs are provided in Section 4.

In Section 5, we present several charts and tables of machine-generated Adams differentials that are particularly relevant to the solution of the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem.

2. Adams E2E_{2} data

2.1. Adams E2E_{2}-pages

Tables 1 provides a list of 49 CW spectra considered in this work, along with the maximum internal degrees computed for the Adams E2E_{2}-pages of the corresponding spectra.

For a CW spectrum X, the Adams E2E_{2}-page data for X is available in the database file X_AdamsSS.db within kervaire_database.zip. Alternatively, the data can be accessed as three plain-text table files:

  • •

    X_AdamsE2_generators.csv (for generators),

  • •

    X_AdamsE2_relations.csv (for relations),

  • •

    X_AdamsE2_basis.csv (for 𝔽2{\mathbb{F}}_{2}-basis).

These files are included in kervaire_csv.rar, available in the Zenodo repository. We illustrate these tables with examples. Tables 2–4 present the first few rows of the corresponding files for the spectrum C2 (the naming convention will be explained later).

Notation 2.1.

In the table of generators, a row with i​d=iid=i is the ii’th generator of the E2E_{2}-page of X. In this section we will denote this generator by xix_{i} if X is a ring spectrum or viv_{i} if X is a module over some ring spectrum (in our dataset there are only two ring spectra S0 and tmf). The columns stem,s are the degrees of the generators. The column name is the latex name we give to the ii’th generator. However, currently not all generators have latex names. The column name might be sometimes vacant (filled with [NULL]).

Notation 2.2.

In the table of relations, consider the column rel for relations. If X is a ring spectrum, then 0,1;1,2,5,4 denotes the relation

x01+x12​x54=0.x_{0}^{1}+x_{1}^{2}x_{5}^{4}=0.

If X is a module over the ring spectra R, then 0,1,3;1,2,5,4,7 denotes the relation

x01​v3+x12​x54​v7=0x_{0}^{1}v_{3}+x_{1}^{2}x_{5}^{4}v_{7}=0

where viv_{i} is the ii’th generator of X and xjx_{j} is the jj’th generator of the ring spectrum R. In summary, the semicolon can be parsed as the plus sign and the monomials are sequences of sub- and upper-scripts whose lengths are even if X is a ring or odd if X is a module. The columns stem,s are the degrees of the relations which can be determined by the degrees of the generators.

Notation 2.3.

In the table of basis, the column mon is parsed in the same way as we parse rel for relations. The only difference is that each mon is a monomial so there should be no semicolon in the column mon. The columns stem,s are the degrees of the monomials. The column index is important. When there are multiple monomial basis elements in the same bidegree, they will be indexed by 0,1,…,k0,1,\dots,k. We write

[i]∈Exts,stem+s​(𝚇)[i]\in\mathrm{Ext}^{\verb|s,stem+s|}(\verb|X|)

to denote the monomial basis element with index ii in Exts,stem+s​(𝚇)\mathrm{Ext}^{\verb|s,stem+s|}(\verb|X|). In the Table of Proofs (see Section 4), the element will be written as

X (stem, s) [i]

in the info column. We can also write [i1,i2,…][i_{1},i_{2},...] to denote the linear combination of monomials with indices i1,i2,…i_{1},i_{2},\dots and [][] to denote the zero element. The d2 column represents the d2d_{2} differentials of the basis elements in the format [i1,i2,…][i_{1},i_{2},...] we just described but in degree (stem-1,s+2). If it is empty, it means that the d2d_{2} differential is trivial. If it is filled with [NULL], it means that the d2d_{2} differential is not calculated yet by the program ./Adams using the secondary Steenrod operations.

Remark 2.5.

All the CW spectra we considered are connective spectra. The current programs only work well with connective spectra.

Remark 2.6.

If there are two or more CW spectra with different homotopy types that satisfy the same naming condition, then the name represents all choices and we do not assume which one we pick. The current important input of the program is the existence of these cofiber sequences and the ones derived from these using the properties of triangulated categories. We will make assumptions on homotopy classes in the future when a new feature of the program is complete and it will enable the ./ss program to rigorously determine if there exists at least one homotopy class that satisfies multiple constraints.

All the CW spectra we consider are known to exist in the literature. One major example is the existence of t​m​ftmf and its 15-skeleton

CW_sigma_nu_eta_2,\verb|CW_sigma_nu_eta_2|,

and we can get many subquotients of CW_sigma_nu_eta_2\verb|CW_sigma_nu_eta_2| and duals of these such as CW_2_eta_nu\verb|CW_2_eta_nu|. The existence of 𝙲𝟸𝚑𝟺,𝙲𝟸𝚑𝟻,𝙲𝟸𝚑𝟼\verb|C2h4|,\verb|C2h5|,\verb|C2h6| is due to the strong Kervaire invariant problem for σ2,θ4,θ5\sigma^{2},\theta_{4},\theta_{5} (See [1] [9]).

2.2. Maps between Adams E2E_{2}-pages

Tables 6–9 give the list of maps between CW spectra we have considered and the maximum computed internal degrees of these maps. The maximum computed internal degree of a map f:X→Σk​Yf:X\to\Sigma^{k}Y refers to the maximum TT such that such that the induced map

f:E2s,t​(X)→E2s+AF⁡(f),t−k+AF⁡(f)​(Y)f:E_{2}^{s,t}(X)\to E_{2}^{s+\mathrm{AF}(f),t-k+\mathrm{AF}(f)}(Y)

is computed in the range t≤Tt\leq T.

For a map X__Y (we will explain the naming later), the data can be found in the database file map_AdamsSS_X_to_Y.db in kervaire_database.zip or in the plain-text table file map_X_to_Y.csv. (A few filenames created by a newer version of ./Adams drop ‘to’ from the names.) Table 10 lists some rows from map_C2_to_C2h4.csv to illustrate the following notation.

Notation 2.7.

In the table of maps, there are only two columns id,map. The map column gives us the image of the id’th generator from E2∗,∗​(X)E_{2}^{*,*}(X) to E2∗,∗​(Y)E_{2}^{*,*}(Y), which is parsed in the same way as we parse rel in the table of relations. For example, we can read from Table 10 that the image of v36∈E2∗,∗​(𝙲𝟸)v_{36}\in E_{2}^{*,*}(\verb|C2|) is

v63+x1​x48​v0∈E2∗,∗​(𝙲𝟸𝚑𝟺).v_{63}+x_{1}x_{48}v_{0}\in E_{2}^{*,*}(\verb|C2h4|).

We explain our naming scheme for these maps.

Notation 2.8.

Let X,Y,Z be names of CW spectra. The following examples demonstrate our naming for the maps between CW spectra.

  • •

    If X has strictly fewer cells than Y and there exists a unique kk and a unique inclusion (up to homotopy) such that X is a subcomplex of Σk\Sigma^{k}Y, then X__Y denotes this subcomplex map X↪Σk\hookrightarrow\Sigma^{k}Y.

  • •

    If X has strictly more cells than Y and there exists a unique kk and a unique quotient such that Σk\Sigma^{k}Y is a quotient complex of X, then X__Y denotes this quotient map X→Σk\to\Sigma^{k}Y.

  • •

    If we have a cofiber sequence

    𝚇→Σm​𝚈→Σn​𝚉→Σ​𝚇\verb|X|\to\Sigma^{m}\verb|Y|\to\Sigma^{n}\verb|Z|\to\Sigma\verb|X|

    whose first map is a subcomplex inclusion denoted by X__Y and whose second map is a quotient map denoted by Y__Z, then the third boundary map is denoted by Z__Q_Y.

  • •

    For key words a,b,c,d,e, the map CW_d_e__CW_a_b_by_c is equivalent to

    CW_d_e__Q_CW_a_b_c_d_e.\verb|CW_d_e__Q_CW_a_b_c_d_e|.

    Similarly, if we have a map with name X__Y_by_c it means that X has a unique bottom cell and Y has a unique top cell and the map attaches the bottom cell of X to the top cell of Y by c. In other words, these two cells form a subquotient of the cofiber of the map which is equivalent to Cc.

  • •

    For numbers n,l,p,q where p<q=n−1<n<lp<q=n-1<n<l, the map RPn_l__RPp_q is equivalent to RPn_l__Q_RPp_l. In other words, the following three maps form a cofiber sequence.

    (RPp_q__RPp_l,RPp_l__RPn_l,RPn_l__RPp_q)(\verb|RPp_q__RPp_l|,~\verb|RPp_l__RPn_l|,~\verb|RPn_l__RPp_q|)
  • •

    In plain-text names, we use the letter m to denote the negative sign. For example, RP1_256__RPm7_0 corresponds to the map

    ℝ​P1256→Σ​ℝ​P−70≃Σ−7​ℝ​P18.{\mathbb{R}}P_{1}^{256}\to\Sigma{\mathbb{R}}P_{-7}^{0}\simeq\Sigma^{-7}{\mathbb{R}}P_{1}^{8}.
  • •

    Note that ℝ​P0n≡S0∨ℝ​P1n{\mathbb{R}}P_{0}^{n}\equiv S^{0}\vee{\mathbb{R}}P_{1}^{n}. We use RP1_256__S0 to denote the truncated Kahn-Priddy map, which is a composition of the following maps.

    ℝ​P1256→ℝ​P0256→Σ​ℝ​P−1−1=S0.{\mathbb{R}}P_{1}^{256}\to{\mathbb{R}}P_{0}^{256}\to\Sigma{\mathbb{R}}P_{-1}^{-1}=S^{0}.
  • •

    S0__tmf and X__tmf_X are the Hurewicz maps.

All the maps except the Hurewicz maps S0__tmf and X__tmf_X we considered are maps in the cofiber sequences generated by inclusions X⊂YX\subset Y of CW complexes, i.e., the homology maps they induce are injective, surjective or trivial.

2.3. Adams d2d_{2} differentials

Table 11 demonstrates the range of d2d_{2} differentials we have computed and used in the computer programs. The maximum internal degree refers to the maximum TT such that all the d2d_{2} differentials of x∈E2s,t≤Tx\in E_{2}^{s,t\leq T} are known for the corresponding CW spectra.

We refer the reader to [3] and [8] for the algorithm that computes d2d_{2} differentials using the secondary Steenrod operations encoded in a differential graded algebra. The first author also implement this algorithm in the program ./Adams. The d2d_{2} data we computed is already contained the table of basis (see Notation 2.3).

The proofs are given in the Table of Proofs (Section 4). The Adams differentials for a spectrum X produced by the machine are available in the database X_AdamsSS.db within kervaire_database.zip. Alternatively, the data can be accessed in the plain-text table file X_AdamsE2_ss.csv within kervaire_csv.rar.

The extensions in a cofiber sequence X__Y__Z are available in the database cofseq_X__Y__Z.db within kervaire_database.zip. Alternatively, the data can be accessed in the plain-text table file cofseq_X__Y__Z.csv within kervaire_csv.rar.

Notation 3.5.

In the table of Adams spectral sequence, columns stem,s refers to the degrees of the elements in the base column. The columns base,diff should be parsed as linear combinations of the monomial basis in the corresponding bidegree. If level=r<5000, the base column is hit by a drd_{r}-differential from diff. If level=10000-r>5000, the base column supports a drd_{r}-differential hitting diff. If level=9000, it means that base is a permanent cycle. If diff is filled with [NULL], it means that the value of diff is undetermined. The reader can see that we assume that all visible nontrivial differentials in the data are of length shorter than 1000.

Notation 3.6.

In the table of extension spectral sequence corresponding to a cofiber sequence

X→𝑓Y→𝑔Z,X\xrightarrow{f}Y\xrightarrow{g}Z,

the column iC=0,1,2 refers to X,Y,Z where base lives respectively. The other columns are similar to those in Notation 3.5. If iC=1 and level=r<5000, then base is hit by an ff-extension which jumps filtration by rr. If iC=1 and level=10000-r>5000, then base supports an gg-extension which jumps filtration by rr.

Remark 3.7.

All the Adams differentials and extensions can be also visually accessed from the website [5].

4. Proofs

In this section we explain the structure and notations in our machine generated proofs. We call it the Table of Proofs. The Table of Proofs is provided in two different forms in the Zenodo repo: a single sqlite3 database file proofs.db and 22 plain-text tables proofs-part1.csv–proofs-part22.csv. The plain-text table is divided into 22 table files because there are more than 21 million rows in the table and some table viewers like Microsoft Excel has a row limit of one million. We encourage the reader to use the open source software DB Browser for SQLite to access the table in proofs.db. This tool can help you quickly search for what you want in big tables. You can also execute advanced SQL queries in the software.

The following are two typical rows in the Table of Proofs.

The first column id refers to the line number in the table. The columns depth and reason refer to the structure of the proof which we will explain in more details later. The column name refers to the name of a CW spectra or a map in a cofiber sequence.

  • •

    If name is the name of a CW spectrum like the first row, then the columns stem,s,r,x,dx refer to an Adams differential of the spectrum. In our example, this is

    d3​([0,2])=[0,1]d_{3}([0,2])=[0,1]

    for

    [0,2]∈E216,107+16​(𝙲𝚎𝚝𝚊)[0,2]\in E_{2}^{16,107+16}(\verb|Ceta|)

    where [0,2][0,2] denotes the linear combination of the 0th and 2nd basis elements in E216,107+16E_{2}^{16,107+16} in the basis table of Ceta and [0,1][0,1] denotes the linear combination in the bidegree that this differential hits.

  • •

    If name is the name of a map in a cofiber sequence, it is of the form X__Y__Z:n where

    𝚇→𝑓Σ?​𝚈→𝑔Σ?​𝚉→ℎΣ​𝚇\verb|X|\xrightarrow{f}\Sigma^{?}\verb|Y|\xrightarrow{g}\Sigma^{?}\verb|Z|\xrightarrow{h}\Sigma\verb|X|

    is a cofiber sequence and n=0,1,2n=0,1,2 correspond to f,g,hf,g,h respectively. The columns stem,s,r,x,dx refer to an extension of the map. In our example (second row of Table 17), consider the cofiber sequence

    𝙲𝚗𝚞→𝑓CW_nu_eta_2→𝑔Σ6​𝙲𝟸→ℎΣ​𝙲𝚗𝚞.\verb|Cnu|\xrightarrow{f}\verb|CW_nu_eta_2|\xrightarrow{g}\Sigma^{6}\verb|C2|\xrightarrow{h}\Sigma\verb|Cnu|.

    The second row of the table indicates that there is a gg-extension from the permanent cycle

    [0]∈E22,15+2​(CW_nu_eta_2)[0]\in E_{2}^{2,15+2}(\verb|CW_nu_eta_2|)

    to the permanent cycle

    [0]∈E24,15+4−6​(𝙲𝟸)[0]\in E_{2}^{4,15+4-6}(\verb|C2|)

    which jumps filtration by r=2r=2.

Next we explain the structure of the Table of Proofs. A typical proof of an Adams differential has the following form.

Proof Structure 4.1.

Assume that the value of an Adams differential dr​(x)d_{r}(x) has four candidates y1,y2,y3,y4y_{1},y_{2},y_{3},y_{4}. (Usually the number of candidates is a power of two.)

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y1d_{r}(x)=y_{1}, propagate (by the Leibniz rule, naturality, …). Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y2d_{r}(x)=y_{2}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y3d_{r}(x)=y_{3}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

Then we can conclude that dr​(x)=y4d_{r}(x)=y_{4}.

The following 4 rows from the Table of Proofs is a concrete form of Proof Structure 4.1.

id depth reason name stem s t r x dx info
325477 1 T Csigma 116 10 126 4 1 3 1,2 proof1
325478 1 T Csigma 116 10 126 4 1 0 0,2 proof2
325479 1 T Csigma 116 10 126 4 1 0,3 0,1 proof3
325480 0 D Csigma 116 10 126 4 1 NULL

Here the depth column can be thought as the nesting level of the latex itemize environment. Rows with reason=`T' correspond to assumptions (‘T’ is a symbol for ‘Try’). Each assumption row has a multi-line proof in the info column which explains why the assumption leads to a contradiction. For example, the actual content of proof1 is the following.

Get Csigma (116,10) d_3[1]=[1,2]. Apply the Leibniz rule with
S0 (0,1) d_3[0]=[] and get Csigma (116,11) d_3[]=[1,2].
However, Csigma (115,14) [1,2] is not in B_2.

In proof1 the element Csigma (115,14) [1,2] refers to the element

[1,2]∈E214,115+14​(𝙲𝚜𝚒𝚐𝚖𝚊).[1,2]\in E_{2}^{14,115+14}(\verb|Csigma|).

Rows with reason=`D' correspond to the conclusions after we rule out enough candidates (‘T’ rows) of the value of Adams differentials or extensions (‘D’ is a symbol for ‘Deduction’).

Microsoft Excel tip: Since the text in the info column usually contains multiple lines, users who view the csv files with Excel should adjust the height of the edit box indicated by the following screenshot in order to view the whole content of the text.

Next we give examples of more complex proofs of Adams differentials.

Proof Structure 4.2.

Assume that the value of an Adams differential dr​(x)d_{r}(x) has four candidates 0,y1,y2,y30,y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=0d_{r}(x)=0, propagate. Assume that dr+1​(x)d_{r+1}(x) has four possible values z1,z2,z3,z4z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},z_{4}.

    • –

      Assume dr+1​(x)=z1d_{r+1}(x)=z_{1}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

    • –

      Assume dr+1​(x)=z2d_{r+1}(x)=z_{2}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

    • –

      Assume dr+1​(x)=z3d_{r+1}(x)=z_{3}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

    • –

      Assume dr+1​(x)=z4d_{r+1}(x)=z_{4}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y1d_{r}(x)=y_{1}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y2d_{r}(x)=y_{2}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

Then we can conclude that dr​(x)=y3d_{r}(x)=y_{3}.

The following 8 rows from the Table of Proofs is an example of Proof Structure 4.2.

id depth reason name stem s t r x dx info
2463208 1 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 4 0 proof1
2463209 2 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 5 0 proof2
2463210 2 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 5 0 3 proof3
2463211 2 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 5 0 0 proof4
2463212 2 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 5 0 0,3 proof5
2463213 1 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 4 0 0 proof6
2463214 1 T CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 4 0 0,3 proof7
2463215 0 D CW_nu_sigma 112 12 124 4 0 3 NULL

The reader can imagine that there could be proofs with even more complex structure. Consider the following.

Proof Structure 4.3.

Assume that the value of an Adams differential dr​(x)d_{r}(x) has four candidates 0,y1,y2,y30,y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=0d_{r}(x)=0, propagate. Assume that dr+1​(x)d_{r+1}(x) has two possible values z,0z,0.

    • –

      Assume dr+1​(x)=zd_{r+1}(x)=z. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

    We get dr+1​(x)=0d_{r+1}(x)=0. Assume that dr+2​(x)d_{r+2}(x) has two possible values w1,w2w_{1},w_{2}.

    • –

      Assume dr+2​(x)=w1d_{r+2}(x)=w_{1}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

    • –

      Assume dr+2​(x)=w2d_{r+2}(x)=w_{2}. Propagate. Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y1d_{r}(x)=y_{1}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

  • •

    If dr​(x)=y2d_{r}(x)=y_{2}, propagate. Get a contradiction.

Then we can conclude that dr​(x)=y3d_{r}(x)=y_{3}.

A proof with the above structure would be 8 rows from the Table of Proofs with (depth, reason)=(1,T), (2,T), (1,D), (2,T), (2,T), (1,T), (1,T), (0,D). If at some point in the proof we got a permanent cycle, we can even make assumptions about the value of extensions. The reader can find such examples in the Table of Proofs.

Next we describe other types of rows that can be computed or derived from former differentials labeled with different reasons.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`d2'. This means that the d2d_{2} differential is calculated by ./Adams using secondary Steenrod operation algorithm.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`N'. This means that we get a differential from a previous one by naturality.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`G'. This means that we get a trivial differential for degree reason.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`XX'. This corresponds to the case that if we have dr−1​(x)=0d_{r-1}(x)=0 then we automatically get dr​(x2)=0d_{r}(x^{2})=0.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`XY'. This corresponds to the case that if we have dr−1​(x)=0d_{r-1}(x)=0 then no matter what dr​(x)d_{r}(x) is (when there are two candidates or more), we always get the same value for dr​(x​y)d_{r}(xy) by Leibniz rule or dr​(f​(x))d_{r}(f(x)) by naturality.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`ToCs'. This means that in the extension spectral sequence, we have tried all possible values of an extension (linear combinations of elements in the E2E_{2}-page) and the outcome is that certain element in the Adams spectral sequence should survive to the E∞E_{\infty}-page and it becomes a summand of the value of the extension.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`OutCsI'. This means that in the extensions spectral sequence, two permanent cycles should be the same on the E∞E_{\infty}-page. Hence the difference dx should be hit by an Adams differential. In those rows the columns stem,s,t refer to the degree of dx in stead of x.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`CsCm'. These are extensions obtained from some simple homotopy relations. For example, if x∈E∞​(S0)x\in E_{\infty}(S^{0}) is the target of an η\eta-extension, then it should detect a ν\nu-torsion (dnν​(η)=0d_{n}^{\nu}(\eta)=0 for all nn) because we know that η⋅ν=0∈π∗​(S0)\eta\cdot\nu=0\in\pi_{*}(S^{0}). The reader can find more property of extensions in [7].

  • •

    Rows with reason=`Syn'. This means that the differential is obtained by the Generalized Leibniz Rule from the former row. The map used in the Generalized Leibniz Rule and the conditions that the machine checked is written in the info column.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`SynCs'. This means that the row is an extension and is obtained by the Generalized Mahowald Trick. The cofiber sequence used in the Generalized Mahowald Trick and the conditions that the machine checked is written in the info column.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`SynIn'. This means that by the Generalized Mahowald Trick we determine that an element in the Adams spectral sequence should be a permanent cycle and become a summand of an extension.

  • •

    Rows with reason=`TI', `DI', `GI'. These are essentially the same as rows with reason=`T', `D', `G' except that the columns stem,s,t refer to the degree of dx in stead of x. For consecutive rows with reason=`TI' the machine are enumerating possible sources of some differential (when we know dx is hit by some drd_{r} differential beforehand) instead of the possible targets and the conclusion row is one with reason=`DI'.

Remark 4.4.

If the reader wants to search for a proof of certain differential, then usually you need to search for the bidegree of the source of the differential with reason=‘D’ or reason=‘T’. Occasionally the machine knows the target should be hit by a certain differential first and deduces the differential by enumerating the possible sources. In this case you also need to search for the bidegree of the target of the differential with reason=‘DI’ or reason=‘TI’.

5. Charts and tables

In this section we list the Adams differentials of S0S^{0} in the range 122≤s​t​e​m≤127122\leq stem\leq 127, 0≤s≤250\leq s\leq 25 and Adams differentials of C​νC\nu in the range s​t​e​m=126stem=126, 9≤s≤149\leq s\leq 14. These differentials would play an important role in our solution of the Last Kervaire Invariant Problem [7].
